AfriScan · Rwanda · Rights of way, projects and licence areas

Know what is built inside your right of way in Rwanda

AfriScan maps structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground along power lines, roads and water mains, and inside mining and project areas. Each feature is measured against the right-of-way widths that apply to your line or site, checked by a person, and delivered as GIS files and a PDF report. Satellite first, with drone detail only where a job needs it and the approvals are in place.

  • Every 500 mRated for encroachment density

The rules behind the work RURA right-of-way guidelines (2015) · Law n° 21/2011 on electricity · Law n° 32/2015 on expropriation · Law n° 27/2021 on land · Law n° 072/2024 on mining · RCAR Part 27 (2026) · Law n° 058/2021 on personal data · World Bank ESS5 · IFC Performance Standard 5

The rule

The right of way is already defined

In Rwanda, the right of way for power lines is set by RURA’s Guidelines N°01/GL/EL-EWS/RURA/2015. We measure each structure against the width for your voltage, or against the easement widths in your file.

The minimum width is 12 m for 15–30 kV lines, 25 m for 110 kV, 30 m for 220 kV and 50 m for 400 kV, with the line centred. The guidelines forbid building or cultivating in the right of way without the licensee’s consent, drilling, mining or excavating in it, fires within 60 m of a transmission right of way, and blasting within 100 m of any power line. They also say the corridor “shall generally be clear of unauthorized structures”. What counts as authorised is for the licensee and the authorities to decide. We show you, with dates, which structures stand within the right of way and how far each is from the line.

Rwanda’s grid is growing on both levels: REG’s June 2023 transmission plan records about 1,156 km of high-voltage lines and lists new 110 kV and 220 kV lines, and World Bank-financed programmes are extending distribution. Every new line needs a route, a right of way and a record of what stood on the land.

What you receive

A dated register your right-of-way, RAP and GIS teams can use

  • Features by band and by segment: for a power line, for example 0–6 m, 6–12.5 m, 12.5–15 m and 15–25 m from the centreline, or your own widths.
  • The distance of each feature to the centreline, with its chainage and coordinates.
  • The image date and source for every feature.
  • Change since your last survey: new and removed structures, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer.
  • GeoPackage, GeoJSON, Shapefile and KMZ layers that load into your GIS, an interactive map file that opens in a browser, and a PDF report in English.

Before valuation

The date a structure appeared matters

Electric lines, roads, water pipes, gas and oil pipelines and mineral resources in the public domain are all activities of public interest under the Expropriation Law (Law n° 32/2015, art. 5). Once an expropriation decision is published, long-term activities started on the land after it “shall not be compensable” (art. 17), and the law gives 30 days for the valuation, extendable by up to 15 days (art. 29).

A 2026 resettlement action plan published by REG observes that “The Rwanda national law is silent on cut-off date”, and adopts the World Bank’s ESS5, so lender-financed projects set one under their own standards. A dated inventory of what stood on each segment, and when, supports the records your RAP team needs. It supports the census and asset inventory; it does not replace them.

Structures, not people

Our registers describe structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks. They carry no names, ID numbers or parcel-owner details, and results go only to the contacts you name. Maps linked to named households are personal data under Law n° 058/2021, so tell us before sharing any.

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks. We do not identify, count or follow people, and whether a structure is authorised is for you and the authorities to decide. Our registers support your right-of-way, engagement and resettlement work; they do not replace any of it.

A person reviews every result

Automatic models and building databases propose; an analyst confirms each feature before it reaches you. What imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Basemaps are never delivered as survey imagery.

Scheduled, never “real‑time”

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice after each one.

Satellite first, drones under Part 27

Satellite first, drone where it adds detail

Most corridor questions can be answered from dated satellite imagery, with no aircraft, no flight and no site visit. Where more detail is needed, drone surveys in Rwanda are subject to RCAA authorisation under Part 27 of the Rwanda Civil Aviation Regulations, and to the security reviews and consents each job requires. High-tension lines, power plants, highways and communication masts are restricted sites, so every flight near them needs explicit RCAA permission.

Afridrone is working towards the approvals Rwanda requires. Every drone proposal sets out the approvals its flights need and who holds each one, so your team can check them.

The Rwanda drone-law guide

Registration, pilot licences, activity permits, the UOC, restricted sites, BVLOS area approvals, privacy and an 11-point checklist for clients, as of 27 September 2026.

Drone law in Rwanda

Where we don't work

The DRC border band is out of scope

In line with current government travel advice, we do not offer field or drone work within 10 km of the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. That band covers most of the Lake Kivu shore and islands and the Rubavu and Rusizi border areas. We also take extra care near the Burundi border, in Nyungwe, on the DRC-border section of Volcanoes National Park and around Kigali’s military zones.

Frequently asked questions

Which right-of-way width do you use?

For power lines, the minimum widths in Schedule I of RURA’s 2015 guidelines, with the line centred, or the easement widths in your file where they differ. For roads, water mains, project footprints and licence areas, the boundary or distances you give us. Up to six widths can be reported in one survey, each structure with its distance to the line and its band.

Which imagery do you use, and from which dates?

Dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold. Every feature carries the name of its imagery source and, where the source gives one, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery or delivered to you.

Do we need a drone survey?

Not usually. Most right-of-way and licence-area questions can be answered from dated satellite imagery, with no flight and no site visit. Where a stretch needs more detail, drone surveys are subject to the RCAA approvals, security reviews and consents each job requires, and high-tension lines are restricted sites under the drone rules. See drone law in Rwanda.

Can you show what was there before a cut-off date?

Where dated archive imagery of your area exists, yes. We tell you what is available, and from which dates, before you commit. When the archive is too old, a new satellite capture can be requested; its date depends on satellite availability and weather.

Can you tell us which structures are unauthorised?

No. We map what stands where, and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether a structure has the licensee’s consent, predates the line or the licence, or is authorised at all is for you and the authorities to decide. The register gives your team a dated, located list to work from.

Do you work near the DRC border?

We do not offer field or drone work within 10 km of the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in line with current government travel advice. That band covers most of the Lake Kivu shore and islands and the Rubavu and Rusizi border areas.

Know what stands on each segment before the valuation starts.

Send the route or boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the District or Districts, and the voltage, right-of-way width or licence-area coordinates. Tell us about any cut-off or valuation date. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
